messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai is a 41-year-old dancer, married, and living in a quiet suburb outside Portland. For three years, he worked as a relief coordinator for a humanitarian organization in a conflict zone, delivering supplies to villages caught between shifting front lines. The event that broke him happened on a late afternoon, just after 4:30 PM. His convoy had stopped at a checkpoint, and a nearby fuel depot had been hit by an artillery shell. The air thickened with the smell of burning diesel, dust, and something else—a burnt, chemical odor he later learned was melted rubber and human remains. He had tried to help a wounded colleague, but the man died in his arms, and Kai froze—unable to move, unable to call for help, unable to do anything but crouch behind a wall while the world burned. For months afterward, he told himself that he should have done more, that his paralysis proved he couldn't be trusted under pressure.

Now, back in the United States, Kai is a dancer for a small contemporary company. The job demands physical precision and emotional openness, but his mind has become a minefield. The late afternoon light slanting through the studio windows is the worst. Every day, around 4:30 PM, the quality of the light shifts, and Kai feels it like a trapdoor opening beneath him. He has come to believe that his reactions since the event prove he is a lousy coper, that he cannot rely on himself to handle even ordinary stress. This belief makes him hypervigilant: he scans the studio for anything that might trigger him—a dancer warming up with a lighter, the smell of someone's lunch reheated in the break room, the faintest whiff of burnt popcorn from the microwave. He is certain that if he lets his guard down, the memory will ambush him, and he will freeze again, just like he did that afternoon.

The triggers do ambush him, without warning. A student brings in a bottle of whiskey for a class celebration, and the alcohol smell hits Kai like a wave—suddenly he is back behind that wall, the burnt smell of the depot filling his nostrils, his heart hammering. He feels the shame wash over him: he acted in ways that go against who he is, he thinks, because he froze instead of helping. The memory does not just replay; it relives. He feels the heat on his skin, hears the distant thud of another shell, and for a long, frozen moment he is not in the studio at all. These episodes reinforce his conviction that he is broken, that his own mind is untrustworthy. He begins to avoid anything that might carry that burnt smell—he refuses to walk past the studio's kitchenette, asks his wife to stop using the toaster, and leaves rehearsals early if someone lights a candle. His company director has noticed. Twice now, Kai has missed key transitions in a new piece because he was standing at the back of the stage, eyes fixed on the floor, waiting for the moment to pass.

The cycle tightens. The more Kai believes he cannot rely on himself, the more he scans for threats, and the more triggers he finds. Each triggered flashback deepens his shame and reinforces his negative appraisals. He has started to avoid the late afternoon entirely—he schedules all his classes for the morning, tells his wife he is too tired for evening walks, and sits in the dark of his living room as the sun goes down, curtains drawn. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in rehearsal last week: the choreographer asked him to hold a pose for thirty seconds, and Kai could not do it. His arms shook, his breath came fast, and he walked off the floor without a word. He is afraid that his career is ending, that he will lose the one thing that still feels like his own. But what frightens him most is the thought that he might be right—that he really cannot rely on himself, and that the shame will never lift.
